background: In August 2026, millions of records allegedly sourced from Chess.com were posted online . The data contained 7.3M rows with 4.6M unique email addresses, along with usernames, names, countries and data relating to users' Chess.com accounts. Analysis of the data suggested it had been obtained by scraping. When loaded into HIBP, 99% of the email addresses had already appeared in previous data breaches, further supporting the scraping theory.
Read more about scrapes and data breaches.
how: Analysis of the data suggested it had been obtained by scraping.
When loaded into HIBP, 99% of the email addresses had already appeared in previous data breaches, further supporting the scraping theory.
outcome: 4,653,212 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Geographic locations, Names, Usernames.
editorial: Two details in this record deserve more weight than the total. The first is that analysis indicated the data was scraped rather than taken from a database, collected through interfaces that were working as designed, at a scale nobody intended. The second is that 99% of the addresses had already appeared in earlier breaches. Both facts cut the same way, and not in the direction most people assume.

A scrape means no password was exposed, so there is nothing to reset. A 99% overlap with previous incidents means almost nobody in this file is newly exposed. If you are in it, this is very unlikely to be the breach that matters to you, one of the earlier ones already was. What it does add is linkage.

A username joined to a real name, a country and a confirmed email address is exactly the material used to connect a pseudonymous account to a person. If your chess handle is one you also use elsewhere, that connection is now easier for anyone to make, and no password change undoes it.

fields.name: Geographic locations
fields.why: Where the account was used, which narrows a person down further than most people expect.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: The address becomes a confirmed, active target, expect more phishing, better aimed.

fields.name: Usernames
fields.why: A handle links this account to every other place the same handle is used.

actions: Expect better-aimed phishing. A message that already knows your name and where you have an account is the whole point of a breach like this.
breach.scale_line: That is about 17% of the population of Australia.
